title: Morwen Bumble and the Sunstone Rudder
markdown:
The Riverbend Canal Festival buzzed harder than a hive that had remembered a holiday. Bunting kingfisher-bright snapped from lampposts. Children ran with paper dragonflies on sticks. The air was a jumble of fried dough, roses, and the wet-wood smell of boats that wanted to be important. Morwen Bumble stood in it with gangly limbs and earnest eyes, trying to look like a sailor on a calm sea and achieving, mostly, sapling in a gust. He smoothed a shirt that was already neat. A beetle considered his boot and thought better of it. He let it go, which felt, briefly, like practice.

Beside him, Grandma Elara, retired botanist, wrote wildflowers into a leather notebook as if the festival might forget them. “Campanula rotundifolia,” she murmured. “Tough. Clings to rock. A lesson in staying.” Morwen nodded and looked toward the backstage anyway.

Behind the main stage the Dragonfly Dash was coming apart the way a parade comes apart: loudly, and with opinions. The giant dragonfly raft, impressive and a little drunk on its own wings, had lost its rudder. Officials argued over a frayed rope and a horn that had gone travelling. One man held the rope as if it might confess. Another accused the river. The jewel of the festival sat on a wobbly edge. Morwen’s stomach flipped. He wanted to step in, to be the knot that held. He also believed, with the faith of a boy who had tripped over his own triumphs, that he was always one peel from disaster. Last spring he had saved a picnic and sat in the pie. If the race failed and he had only watched, his palms would stay clammy until winter.

“Every petal has its season,” Elara said. “But disappointed faces make a poor garden. If they cancel, the experiment fails before it starts.” She nudged his elbow, moth-light.

“I’ll go,” Morwen said, a little too loud, and slid under the velvet rope with her glance as permission.

Backstage was a nest of forgotten things and anxious feet. Wires snagged his trousers with tiny persistent tugs. A crate of paper flowers had shed a spring. He stepped around a bucket, then around his own doubt. A stagehand wrestled a banner like a badger with a principle. “A rudder?” Morwen asked, voice aiming for oak and arriving as sapling. “For the Dash. Special.”

“Shiny thing,” the stagehand said, not looking up. “Vital, they said. Off to the Silent Symphony tents. Madame Fleur has probably glued it to a peony.”

Madame Fleur. Prize dahlias. School corridors once flooded with trophies had never managed this particular awe, or this particular terror. Morwen walked, leaves crunching opinions under his shoes. The Silent Symphony tent sat apart, as if noise were a weed. A sign in perfect script asked visitors to whisper. He whispered an apology to a daisy that had not asked.

Inside, lilies and ferns stood as if they had been given instructions and intended to follow them for the rest of their lives. Each frond had an angle. The air smelled expensive and slightly sad, the way cut flowers do when they know the hour. Among white orchids, catching light like a held star, lay the Sunstone: amber oval, gold inlay, the raft’s missing will. It looked innocent. It looked like a theft that had been arranged by taste.

“Madame Fleur,” Morwen said, tremor included. “That stone steers the Dragonfly Dash.”

She turned a gaze that could wilt a rose that was already trying. “Rudder? This is the jewel of my Symphony of the Dawn. Weeks to find a brightness like this. It is certainly not a rudder.”

He felt the old public-failure weather roll in, the particular damp of being looked at while dropping something important. He could fetch Elara and hide among sensible specimens, Latin names like a blanket. He pictured the canal without cheers, the dragonfly raft a joke with wings. He remembered her twinkle when she said the experiment would fail before it started. He stayed. His feet argued. He won, narrowly.

“It is,” he said. “It helps the raft turn. It is important.” The words came in a rush. She listened with a face like closed petals.

“And what,” she asked, sharp enough for stems, “do you offer for my dawn?”

He thought of the Best Floating Sculpture, parked on a crate near the flower tents because he had wanted it near beauty. Days of reeds. Afternoons of dandelion fluff that refused to behave. A miniature boat with a honey-cake sail, the one work he had not rushed, the quiet proof that he could finish a thing without knocking it over. Looking at her, and at the race that needed a spine, he knew the price. The sculpture was the only triumph he trusted. The Dash was everyone else’s afternoon.

“My sculpture,” he said. “Almost finished. Take it.” The sweet smell of petals that had begun to tire found his eyes. He held out the little boat. Hands, not quite steady. “Please.”

She studied him as if he were a root system. “A worthy exchange. Take your rudder. Bring me the sculpture.” A dewdrop of a smile, almost.

He ran with the Sunstone warm in his palm, perfume and wilted roses falling behind like a tide that had changed its mind. A paper dragonfly stuck to his sleeve; he left it. The towpath was elbows and spilled lemonade. The chief organiser, thunder-faced, had opened his mouth on cancel. A child had already begun to cry in a practised way.

“Wait,” Morwen called, holding the stone up so the gold could argue for him. Festival workers, suddenly willing, helped him seat it in the dragonfly’s tail. It clicked as if it had been sulking, not lost. Late sun found the inlay and threw it back along the water, a brief second afternoon. The cheer came like weather deciding to be kind. Someone clapped his shoulder too hard. He did not drop anything.

He watched the Dash from the bank, not as a captain, as a boy who had chosen. The dragonfly went smooth, a ridiculous insect doing a serious job. The ache for the reed boat sat beside the satisfaction and did not spoil it. Elara arrived with a sprig of campanula and did not lecture. The horn, wherever it had gone, was no longer required.

That evening the lights on the canal were fallen stars that had agreed to stay low. Music leaked from a barge and then thought better of it. Morwen sat on the wall and held one leftover dandelion seed, a leftover because the sculpture’s mast had shed. A breeze took it. A beetle crossed his shoe; a bird came too close; he observed both without disaster, which was, for him, a kind of medal. Elara’s smile was small and botanical. She did not mention forests or promises. He did not need her to. He already knew the seed had gone where it meant to, and that he had too. Across the water the dragonfly raft slept against its rope, Sunstone dull now, work done.
characters: Morwen (child who is always one step from triumph and one peel from disaster), Elara (a grandmother who finds this all very educational)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic adventure story for older children
